ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there is a vertical dashed line labeled as the z axis, and the arrows of magnetic field B are radially distributed outward from near the z axis within a horizontal circular cross-section. On the right side there is a black vertical conductor rod, the conductor rod is parallel to the z axis, and its length is marked beside it as 1 m; the horizontal distance from the z axis to the conductor rod is also marked as 1 m. Reasoning: The problem gives B = 1 T, and the needed induced voltage e = 1 V. When the conductor rotates around the z axis, its velocity direction is tangential, and the magnitude is v = ωr. The magnetic field direction is radial, and the direction of the conductor element dl is vertical, therefore (v × B) is along the conductor direction, and the magnitude is constant along the rod. Using the motional emf formula e = ∫(v × B)·dl, one can obtain e = BωrL. Substituting B = 1 T, r = 1 m, L = 1 m, e = 1 V: 1 = 1·ω·1·1, so ω = 1 rad/s. Converting to rpm: N = ω·60/(2π) = 60/(2π) ≈ 9.55 rpm.

method.method_draft: First identify from the image that the conductor is a vertical rod at fixed radius 1 m from the z-axis and that B is radial. From the text take B = 1 T, rod length L = 1 m, required emf e = 1 V. Since the rod rotates about the z-axis, its velocity is tangential with magnitude ωr. Use the motional-emf integral e = ∫(v × B)·dl; because v is tangential, B is radial, and dl is vertical, the magnitude is constant along the rod: e = BωrL. Solve for ω and convert rad/s to rpm to get 9.55 rpm.
